claims.source: In support of this idea, the simultaneous tracking of DFCs and EVL cells revealed that the speed, direction, and extent of DFC vegetal movement tightly matched the vegetal spreading of the EVL (Figure 3D–G; Figure 3—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—video 1.

claims.claim: DFCs and overlying EVL cells share the same bias in the orientation of the elongation axis.
claims.source: Furthermore, DFCs and overlying EVL cells shared the same bias in the orientation of the elongation axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating a morphogenetic coupling between the two tissues.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Contraction and friction-based flows of a ring-like YSL actomyosin network drive YSL/EVL vegetal spreading during epiboly.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that contraction and friction-based flows of a ring-like YSL actomyosin network drive YSL/EVL vegetal spreading during epiboly (Behrndt et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2004; Heisenberg and Bellaiche, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Behrndt et al., 2012, Cheng et al., 2004, and Heisenberg and Bellaiche, 2013.

claims.claim: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 show a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading.
claims.source: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 (MYPT1) showed a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading. Likewise, DFCs decreased their vegetal ward speed to the same extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: DFCs decrease their vegetal ward speed to the same extent as YSL/EVL in embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1.
claims.source: Embryos expressing N-ter-MYPT1 (MYPT1) showed a speed drop in YSL/EVL vegetalward spreading. Likewise, DFCs decreased their vegetal ward speed to the same extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreases the speed of EVL spreading.
claims.source: Similarly, local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreased the speed of EVL spreading, as previously shown (Behrndt et al., 2012), simultaneously decreasing the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—video 1, and a citation to Behrndt et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments simultaneously decreases the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone.
claims.source: Similarly, local disruption by laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring in direct contact with marginal DFC apical attachments decreased the speed of EVL spreading, as previously shown (Behrndt et al., 2012), simultaneously decreasing the speed of DFC vegetal movement near the ablated zone (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4A, Figure 4B, and Figure 4—video 1.

claims.claim: The progress of DFC vegetal movement requires the vegetal spreading of the extra-embryonic YSL/EVL.
claims.source: Together, these results demonstrate that the progress of DFC vegetal movement requires the vegetal spreading of the extra-embryonic YSL/EVL.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that disrupting YSL/EVL spreading decreases DFC vegetal movement speed.

claims.claim: Apical attachments and DFCs are under vegetally directed tension.
claims.source: We observed that apical attachments recoiled towards the animal pole after ablation, triggering a fast retraction of the DFC body, indicating that both apical attachments and DFCs were under vegetally directed tension (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: The constricted cortical zone induced by wound repair pulls apical attachments towards the vegetal pole, restoring the vegetal directionality of DFC movement.
claims.source: Subsequently, the constricted cortical zone induced by wound repair pulled apical attachments towards the vegetal pole, restoring the vegetal directionality of DFC movement, further indicating that apical attachments are able to transmit motion information from the EVL to DFCs (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser ablation data presented in Figure 4D, Figure 4E, and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: Isolated individual DFCs devoid of apical attachments move without persistence and directionality, even towards the animal pole in the opposite direction to the vegetal movement of the YSL/EVL.
claims.source: In these 'natural' experiments, we observed that isolated individual DFCs devoid of apical attachments (hereafter referred to as 'detached DFCs') moved without persistence and directionality, even towards the animal pole in the opposite direction to the vegetal movement of the YSL/EVL (Figure 5B–E; Figure 4—video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5B–E and Figure 4—video 3.

claims.claim: Isolated individual DFCs connected with the extra-embryonic tissues by apical attachments show a persistent and directed movement toward the vegetal pole, mimicking the movement of extra-embryonic tissues.
claims.source: In contrast, isolated individual DFCs connected with the extra-embryonic tissues by apical attachments (hereafter referred to as 'attached DFCs') showed a persistent and directed movement toward the vegetal pole, mimicking the movement of extra-embryonic tissues (Figure 5B–E; Figure 4—video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5B–E and Figure 4—video 3.

claims.claim: The persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlate with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments.
claims.source: Importantly, the persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlated with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments (Figure 5G and H), and this close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements (Figure 5F–I) was only lost upon detachment (Figure 5E; Figure 4—video 3), indicating the requirement of physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 5G, Figure 5H, Figure 5F–I, Figure 5E, and Figure 4—video 3.

claims.claim: Physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues is required for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
claims.source: Importantly, the persistence and speed of movement of DFCs correlated with the persistence and speed of movement of apical attachments (Figure 5G and H), and this close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements (Figure 5F–I) was only lost upon detachment (Figure 5E; Figure 4—video 3), indicating the requirement of physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the close spatial and temporal relationship between apical attachments and DFC movements is only lost upon detachment.

claims.claim: Apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, guiding their vegetal movement during epiboly.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, guiding their vegetal movement during epiboly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues is required for the persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs.

claims.claim: In 55% of embryos, often one or two, and up to five detached DFCs per embryo leave the cluster as single cells.
claims.source: We observed that in 55% of embryos, often one or two, and up to five detached DFCs per embryo left the cluster as single cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Detached DFCs that leave the cluster move mainly in direction to the animal pole, being sequestered by the internalisation movement of the DCL and incorporating into this embryonic cell layer.
claims.source: These cells moved mainly in direction to the animal pole, being sequestered by the internalisation movement of the DCL and incorporating into this embryonic cell layer (Figure 6B; Figure 6—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6B and Figure 6—video 1.

claims.claim: Detached DFCs that are sequestered by the DCL mimic the morphology and movement behaviour of endodermal cells and at later stages differentiate in endodermal tissue derivatives.
claims.source: Remarkably, this group of DFCs mimicked the morphology and movement behaviour of endodermal cells and at later stages differentiated in endodermal tissue derivatives (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: DFCs transplanted into the paraxial region of host embryos follow endodermal cell fate and form endodermal tissue derivatives.
claims.source: Furthermore, DFCs transplanted into the paraxial region of host embryos, where endodermal and mesodermal progenitors develop, also followed endodermal cell fate and form endodermal tissue derivatives (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by transplantation data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At the onset of epiboly, the entire population of DFCs are transiting the process of delamination and thus are all attached to the YSL and EVL.
claims.source: Immunostaining for ZO-1 and F-actin revealed that at the onset of epiboly the entire population of DFCs were transiting the process of delamination and thus were all attached to the YSL and EVL (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: As epiboly progresses, detached DFCs steadily increase to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly.
claims.source: However, as epiboly progressed, detached DFCs steadily increased to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly, and by 90% epiboly they became the predominant pool of DFCs (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: By 90% epiboly, detached DFCs become the predominant pool of DFCs.
claims.source: However, as epiboly progressed, detached DFCs steadily increased to outnumber the attached DFC population from around 75% epiboly, and by 90% epiboly they became the predominant pool of DFCs (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The progressive increase of detached cells is due to DFCs completing the process of delamination and events of cell division.
claims.source: Through time-lapse microscopy, we found that the progressive increase of detached cells was not only due to DFCs completing the process of delamination (Figure 3B), but detached DFCs also emerged from events of cell division (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 3B, Figure 6D, and Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The entire population of DFCs moves in direction to the vegetal pole in coordination with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues until advanced stages of epiboly.
claims.source: As previously noted, despite the continuous increase in the number of detached DFCs (Figure 6E), the entire population of DFCs still moved in direction to the vegetal pole in coordination with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues until advanced stages of epiboly (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Around 85–90% of epiboly, when the percentage of detached cells reaches 80%, the DFC cluster detaches from the EVL and significantly lowers its vegetal movement.
claims.source: Only around 85–90% of epiboly, when the percentage of detached cells reached 80%, the DFC cluster detached from the EVL and significantly lowered its vegetal movement (Figure 6E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claims.claim: DFCs change from being a collection of dispersed progenitors to a tightly packed cellular cluster during epiboly.
claims.source: During epiboly, DFCs change from being a collection of dispersed progenitors to a tightly packed cellular cluster (Figure 1A; Figure 1—video 1; Oteiza et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1, and a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008.

claims.claim: DFC clustering is achieved by progressively decreasing the distance between progenitors and increasing the contact with the surrounding cells.
claims.source: Quantitative assessment of collective cell behaviour revealed that DFC clustering was achieved by progressively decreasing the distance between progenitors and increasing the contact with the surrounding cells (Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7A and Figure 7B.

claims.claim: DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA.
claims.source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kane et al., 2005 and immunostaining data presented in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: DFCs localise E-cadherin at the cell membrane.
claims.source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Functional abrogation of E-cadherin affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly.
claims.source: During this process, DFCs express e-cadherin mRNA (Kane et al., 2005) and also localise E-cad at the cell membrane (Figure 7E), and previous reports have shown that functional abrogation of this adhesion molecule affects the cluster cohesion of DFCs leading to a scattered organisation of DFCs at 90% of epiboly (Oteiza et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2010.

claims.claim: E-cadherin knockdown disrupts cluster cohesion, leading to multiple racemes of DFCs that move in the vegetal direction guided by their apical attachments with the YSL and EVL.
claims.source: We found that E-cad knockdown disrupted cluster cohesion, leading to multiple racemes of DFCs that moved in the vegetal direction guided by their apical attachments with the YSL and EVL (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL increases significantly in E-cadherin knockdown embryos.
claims.source: Remarkably, the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL increased significantly in these embryos (Figure 7G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 7G and Figure 7H.

claims.claim: E-cadherin-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs, avoiding cell escape and promoting the formation of a tight cellular cluster.
claims.source: These results indicate that E-cad-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs, avoiding cell escape and promoting the formation of a tight cellular cluster.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin knockdown disrupts cluster cohesion and increases the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group.

claims.claim: In 57% of embryos, the DFC population organises as a single cell cluster from early stages of vegetal movement.
claims.source: We observed that the DFC population organised as a single cell cluster from early stages of vegetal movement in 57% of embryos (Figure 8A and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data presented in Figure 8A and Figure 8C.

claims.claim: In 43% of embryos, DFCs initially form two (28%) or three (15%) small cell clusters separated by an average distance of 50 µm, which only at later stages of epiboly coalesce to form a single cluster.
claims.source: However, in the remaining 43% of embryos, DFCs initially formed two (28%) or three (15%) small cell clusters separated by an average distance of 50 µm, which only at later stages of epiboly coalesced to form a single cluster (Figure 8B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data presented in Figure 8B–D.

claims.claim: DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiate adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions that result in the establishment of long-term adhesion between cells, allowing DFC clustering.
claims.source: Our time-lapse image analysis revealed that DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiated adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions that resulted in the establishment of long-term adhesion between cells, allowing DFC clustering (Figure 8E; Figure 8—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8E and Figure 8—video 1.

claims.claim: The protrusions involved in DFC clustering differ from other protrusions formed by DFCs by their longer length, increased lifetime, and alignment between clusters.
claims.source: The protrusions involved in this process differed from other protrusions formed by DFCs not only by their longer length, but also by their increased lifetime and alignment between clusters (Figure 8F–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 8F–I.

claims.claim: Long-range cell-cell contact interactions mediated by polarised protrusions function as seeds for the establishment of stable adhesion between DFCs.
claims.source: Collectively, these results indicate that long-range cell-cell contact interactions mediated by polarised protrusions function as seeds for the establishment of stable adhesion between DFCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DFCs located at the edges of distant cell clusters initiate adhesive contacts by sending out long polarised protrusions.

claims.claim: Subsets of small clusters of DFCs that contain several cells with apical attachments begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.
claims.source: Remarkably, using transgenic embryos expressing a fluorescent biosensor for F-actin only in DFCs, we observed a temporal connection between the formation of protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts and the loss of apical attachments. Subsets of small clusters of DFCs that contained several cells with apical attachments began to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs (Figure 8J – 0–16 min; Figure 8—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8J and Figure 8—video 2.

claims.claim: Small clusters of DFCs complete the delamination process when fully integrated into the central DFC cluster.
claims.source: Subsequently, they completed the delamination process when fully integrated into the central DFC cluster (Figure 8J – 23–47 min; Figure 8—video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 8J and Figure 8—video 2.

claims.claim: Cell-cell contact interactions between DFCs integrate detached cells into the vegetal movement of attached cells to guide the clustering and directional vegetal movement of the entire DFC collective.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings indicate that cell-cell contact interactions between DFCs integrate detached cells into the vegetal movement of attached cells to guide the clustering and directional vegetal movement of the entire DFC collective.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claims.claim: Incomplete delamination serves as a cellular platform for coordinated tissue movements during development.
claims.source: Thus, we reveal that incomplete delamination serves as a cellular platform for coordinated tissue movements during development.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments derived from incomplete delamination guide the vegetal movement of DFCs.

claims.claim: The apical constriction process underlying the delamination of DFC progenitors follows a temporal progression that allows these cells to retain long-term apical attachments with the EVL and YSL as they spread towards the vegetal pole during epiboly.
claims.source: Remarkably, the apical constriction process underlying the delamination of DFC progenitors follows a temporal progression that allows these cells to retain long-term apical attachments with the EVL and YSL as they spread towards the vegetal pole during epiboly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the kinetics of apical area reduction varies among cells and results in discrete apical attachments that connect these cells with the YSL and EVL for extended periods.

claims.claim: Apical attachments work as tissue connectors that couple DFCs with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues, guiding their motion towards the site of differentiation at the vegetal pole.
claims.source: Apical attachments work as tissue connectors that couple DFCs with the vegetal spreading of extra-embryonic tissues, guiding their motion towards the site of differentiation at the vegetal pole.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs.

claims.claim: Mechanical drag by extra-embryonic tissue movement provides the critical guidance cues for DFC directed locomotion.
claims.source: In contrast with previous hypotheses indicating that autonomous motility (Ablooglu et al., 2010) and contact-mediated repulsive interactions with the marginal DCL (Zhang et al., 2016) drive DFC vegetal movement, we show that mechanical drag by extra-embryonic tissue movement provides the critical guidance cues for DFC directed locomotion.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments are required to transmit vegetal spreading from extra-embryonic tissues to attached DFCs, and is contrasted with previous hypotheses.

claims.claim: Incomplete delamination serves as a generic mechanism for coordinated tissue movement during development, driving the allocation of newly formed mesenchymal cell groups.
claims.source: Here, we show that besides this canonical function, incomplete delamination serves as a generic mechanism for coordinated tissue movement during development, driving the allocation of newly formed mesenchymal cell groups.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that incomplete delamination allows DFCs to coordinate their movement with adjacent extra-embryonic tissues.

claims.claim: Asynchrony in apical constriction generates two distinct populations of progenitors: one holding apical attachments and being pulled by the vegetal movement of extra-embryonic tissues, and a second population of detached delaminated DFCs that follows the vegetal movement of apically attached DFCs through DFC-DFC contact mechanisms.
claims.source: Apical attachments guiding DFC movement arise from a process of apical constriction that is asynchronous among DFCs. We show that such asynchrony generates two distinct populations of progenitors, one holding apical attachments and being pulled by the vegetal movement of extra-embryonic tissues, and a second population of detached delaminated DFCs that follows the vegetal movement of apically attached DFCs through DFC-DFC contact mechanisms.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the onset of apical constriction and the time of detachment leading to delamination are highly variable in the DFC population.

claims.claim: Having an asynchronous process of cell delamination potentially increases the chances of maintaining a minimal number of apically attached DFCs able to carry the detached DFC population along their movements.
claims.source: In the context of these evolving two populations, having an asynchronous process of cell delamination potentially increases the chances of maintaining a minimal number of apically attached DFCs able to carry the detached DFC population along their movements, a factor that becomes relevant as epiboly progresses and the ratio of attached/detached DFCs decreases.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential benefit of asynchronous delamination.

claims.claim: Having asynchrony in a collective process of apical constriction promotes the even dissipation of mechanical stress over time and space, protecting the integrity of the epithelium.
claims.source: Furthermore, as apical constriction imposes mechanical stress along the epithelial plane (Heer and Martin, 2017; Martin and Goldstein, 2014), we can speculate that having asynchrony in a collective process of apical constriction promotes the even dissipation of mechanical stress over time and space, protecting the integrity of the epithelium.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential benefit of asynchronous apical constriction, supported by citations to Heer and Martin, 2017 and Martin and Goldstein, 2014.

claims.claim: Delaminated DFCs are intrinsically motile and can move towards the DCL, being sequestered by the massive internalisation movements of this embryonic cellular domain during gastrulation.
claims.source: Delaminated DFCs are intrinsically motile and can move towards the DCL, being sequestered by the massive internalisation movements of this embryonic cellular domain during gastrulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data showing detached DFCs moving towards the DCL.

claims.claim: When DFCs reach the DCL, either during normal development or after transplantation, they follow the endodermal path revealing that DFCs have a previously unrecognised potential to become endoderm that is expressed if they enter the developmental field of the endoderm.
claims.source: Importantly, when DFCs reach the DCL, either during normal development or after transplantation, they follow the endodermal path revealing that DFCs have a previously unrecognised potential to become endoderm that is expressed if they enter the developmental field of the endoderm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging and transplantation data showing DFCs differentiating into endodermal tissue derivatives.

claims.claim: DFCs transiting the process of delamination avoid endodermal fate by establishing E-cadherin-mediated adhesive contacts with the sub-population of attached DFCs before completing the process of delamination.
claims.source: Here, we show that DFCs transiting the process of delamination avoid endodermal fate by establishing E-cad-mediated adhesive contacts with the sub-population of attached DFCs before completing the process of delamination.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claims.claim: DFC-DFC contact interactions mediated by E-cadherin play a dual function: to protect delaminated cells from escaping towards the endoderm and to ensure they move together with the attached DFC population as a collective group.
claims.source: Thus, DFC-DFC contact interactions mediated by E-cad play a dual function, to protect delaminated cells from escaping towards the endoderm and to ensure they move together with the attached DFC population as a collective group.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin knockdown increases the number of detached cells exiting the DFC group towards the DCL.

claims.claim: DFCs located at long distances establish adhesive contacts by sending long polarised protrusions whose persistence and directionality differ from the other short-lived random protrusions formed by most DFCs.
claims.source: Importantly, DFCs located at long distances establish adhesive contacts by sending long polarised protrusions whose persistence and directionality differ from the other short-lived random protrusions formed by most DFCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing that long inter-cluster protrusions differ in length, lifetime, and alignment from other protrusions.

claims.claim: Migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs.
claims.source: Notably, recent work shows that migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs (Jiang et al., 2019), thus opening the possibility that long polarised protrusions are a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by these guidance molecules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Long polarised protrusions may be a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by Cxcl12a/b guidance molecules.
claims.source: Notably, recent work shows that migrasomes containing the chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b become enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs (Jiang et al., 2019), thus opening the possibility that long polarised protrusions are a manifestation of a chemoattraction mechanism mediated by these guidance molecules.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential mechanism underlying long polarised protrusions, supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Small sub-groups of DFCs delaminate only after establishing adhesive contacts with the main DFC cluster, suggesting a mechanistic coupling between cell adhesion, cell motility, and the process of delamination.
claims.source: It is also remarkable the observation that small sub-groups of DFCs delaminate only after establishing adhesive contacts with the main DFC cluster suggesting a mechanistic coupling between cell adhesion, cell motility, and the process of delamination.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that small clusters of DFCs begin to detach from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated adhesive contacts with the central cluster of attached DFCs.

claims.claim: E-cadherin mediates the transfer of movement information between two distinct populations of progenitor cells defined by their state in the delamination process: attached (transiting delamination) and detached (delaminated).
claims.source: Together, these findings provide a novel developmental function for E-cad, mediating the transfer of movement information between two distinct populations of progenitor cells defined by their state in the delamination process: attached (transiting delamination) and detached (delaminated).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that E-cadherin-mediated DFC-DFC adhesion is necessary for the recruitment of detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs.

claims.claim: Motion transfer from attached to detached DFCs resembles the leader-to-follower motion transmission observed in events of collective cell locomotion, many of which also require cadherin-dependent cell-cell contact interactions.
claims.source: Remarkably, motion transfer from attached to detached DFCs resembles the leader-to-follower motion transmission observed in events of collective cell locomotion, many of which also require cadherin-dependent cell-cell contact interactions (Friedl and Gilmour, 2009; Reig et al., 2014; Theveneau and Mayor, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Friedl and Gilmour, 2009, Reig et al., 2014, and Theveneau and Mayor, 2013.

claims.claim: The role of E-cadherin in motion transmission complements the previously described function in clusterisation.
claims.source: In the case of DFCs, the role of E-cad in motion transmission complements the previously described function in clusterisation (Hong and Dawid, 2009; Matsui et al., 2011; Oteiza et al., 2010), and together ensure that progenitors reach the site of terminal differentiation in a sufficient number and organised as a tight collective, a prerequisite to proceed into further stages of organogenesis (Oteiza et al., 2010; Oteiza et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hong and Dawid, 2009, Matsui et al., 2011, Oteiza et al., 2010, and Oteiza et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism of DFC leader-to-follower locomotion works until the percentage of attached cells falls below the 20% limit, around 85–90% of epiboly.
claims.source: It is worth mentioning that the proposed mechanism of DFC leader-to-follower locomotion works until the percentage of attached cells falls below the 20% limit, around 85–90% of epiboly.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing that the DFC cluster detaches from the EVL and significantly lowers its vegetal movement when the percentage of detached cells reaches 80%.

claims.claim: After 85–90% of epiboly, the DFC cluster loses its physical connections with the YSL and EVL and begins an internal cellular reorganisation process leading to rosette formation and organ differentiation.
claims.source: After this stage, the DFC cluster loses its physical connections with the YSL and EVL and begins an internal cellular reorganisation process leading to rosette formation and organ differentiation (Oteiza et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oteiza et al., 2008.

claims.claim: During the transition after 85–90% of epiboly, the DFC cluster continues a vegetal displacement until the end of epiboly but at a slower rate and becomes covered by the DCL.
claims.source: During this transition, the DFC cluster continues a vegetal displacement until the end of epiboly but at a slower rate and becomes covered by the DCL.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing that the DFC cluster continues to move vegetally after detaching from the EVL, but at a slower rate.

claims.claim: Drag-mediated locomotion is a crucial driver of organogenesis that emerges at the interface of embryonic and extra-embryonic cellular domains.
claims.source: Here, we show that drag-mediated locomotion is a crucial driver of organogenesis that emerges at the interface of embryonic and extra-embryonic cellular domains highlighting the essential role of mechanical information from extra-embryonic tissues in driving early embryo development (Christodoulou et al., 2019; Hiramatsu et al., 2013; Reig et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that apical attachments guide the vegetal movement of DFCs, and is supported by citations to Christodoulou et al., 2019, Hiramatsu et al., 2013, and Reig et al., 2017.

results.result: DFCs originate from dorsal EVL cells through an apical constriction-mediated delamination process that is asynchronous among cells. During this process, EVL cells fated to become DFCs progressively reduce their apical area while moving beneath the epithelial sheet, leaving discrete apical attachments enriched in ZO-1 and F-actin that connect delaminating cells with the YSL and EVL for extended periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 provide direct immunostaining evidence (Figure 1D) showing progressive apical area reduction with ZO-1/F-actin enrichment. Claims C15-C18 provide live imaging data (Figure 1E-I) demonstrating variable kinetics of apical constriction and long-term retention of apical attachments. The inference that this represents apical constriction-mediated delamination (C13-C14) is well-supported by the morphological progression observed. The data quality appears robust with appropriate controls.

results.result: DFCs form dynamic membrane protrusions that are enriched at the rear (lateral and animal) edges rather than at the leading (vegetal) edge of the cluster. Inhibition of actin-based protrusions through Rac1-T17N expression eliminates lamellar and filopodial protrusions but does not prevent persistent collective vegetal movement of DFCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 are supported by quantitative protrusion analysis (Figure 2A-D) showing enrichment at rear edges. Claim C23-C24 provide functional evidence through Rac1-T17N perturbation (Figure 2F-K) demonstrating that protrusion-based motility is not required for directional movement. This effectively rules out the prior hypothesis (C20) that polarized protrusions drive DFC vegetal movement. The experimental design is appropriate and the conclusion is logically sound.

results.result: DFCs travel over 350 μm toward the vegetal pole during the delamination process, with highly variable timing of apical constriction onset and detachment among individual cells. The speed, direction, and extent of DFC vegetal movement tightly match the vegetal spreading of the EVL, and DFCs share the same bias in elongation axis orientation as overlying EVL cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by quantitative tracking data (Figure 3B-C) showing travel distance and temporal variability. Claims C27-C28 provide correlation analysis (Figure 3D-G, Pearson's r = 0.97552) and morphometric data (Figure 3—supplement 1) demonstrating tight coupling between DFC and EVL movements. The high correlation coefficient and shared morphological features provide strong evidence for mechanical coupling, though causality requires additional perturbation experiments (provided in subsequent results).

results.result: The vegetal spreading of YSL/EVL, driven by contraction of a ring-like YSL actomyosin network, is required for DFC vegetal movement. Inhibition of YSL actomyosin contractility through N-ter-MYPT1 expression or local laser ablation of the YSL actomyosin ring simultaneously decreases both EVL spreading and DFC vegetal movement speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 provide genetic perturbation evidence (Figure 4—supplement 1C-D) showing coordinated speed reduction in both YSL/EVL and DFCs. Claims C32-C33 provide acute mechanical perturbation through laser ablation (Figure 4A-B) with similar results. The convergence of genetic and physical perturbations strongly supports the causal requirement (C34). However, the N-ter-MYPT1 experiments lack quantification of statistical significance in the main text, and sample sizes should be reported more clearly.

results.result: Apical attachments and DFCs are under vegetally directed tension. Laser ablation of EVL cortical junctions causes apical attachments to recoil toward the animal pole, triggering fast DFC body retraction. Subsequently, wound repair-induced cortical constriction pulls apical attachments back toward the vegetal pole, restoring vegetal directionality of DFC movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by laser ablation experiments (Figure 4C-E, Figure 4—video 2) showing recoil dynamics and recovery. The biphasic response (initial recoil followed by vegetal recovery) provides strong evidence that apical attachments are under tension and can transmit mechanical forces. The kymograph analysis (Figure 4E) clearly demonstrates the temporal dynamics. This is a well-designed experiment that directly tests force transmission.

results.result: Physical attachment to extra-embryonic tissues through apical attachments is required for persistent directed vegetal movement of DFCs. Isolated detached DFCs move without persistence or directionality, while isolated attached DFCs show persistent vegetal movement. The persistence and speed of DFC movement correlate strongly with the persistence and speed of apical attachment movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 provide comparative analysis of naturally occurring isolated attached vs. detached DFCs (Figure 5B-E). Claim C39 provides quantitative correlation analysis (Figure 5G-H) showing strong relationships between DFC and apical attachment movement parameters. The 'natural experiment' approach is elegant, though sample sizes (n=17 attached, n=20 detached from 8 embryos) are modest. The correlation data strongly support the mechanical coupling hypothesis, though the inference of 'requirement' (C40-C41) would be strengthened by experimental detachment of apical attachments.

results.result: In 55% of embryos, detached DFCs can leave the cluster as single cells (1-5 per embryo), moving toward the animal pole and being sequestered by the DCL. These escaped DFCs mimic endodermal cell morphology and behavior, differentiating into endodermal tissue derivatives. Transplantation experiments confirm that DFCs have previously unrecognized potential to adopt endodermal fate when entering the endodermal developmental field.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide quantitative data on escape frequency (Figure 6A-B). Claims C44-C45 provide fate-mapping evidence through long-term imaging (Figure 6—supplement 1A) and transplantation experiments (Figure 6—supplement 1B). The convergence of observational and experimental approaches strongly supports the conclusion that DFCs have endodermal potential. However, the criteria for distinguishing escaped DFCs from native endodermal cells (described in Methods) should be validated more rigorously, as both express sox17::GFP.

results.result: At epiboly onset, all DFCs are attached to YSL/EVL, but detached DFCs steadily increase through completion of delamination and cell division, outnumbering attached DFCs from ~75% epiboly and becoming predominant by 90% epiboly. Despite this increase in detached cells, the entire DFC population maintains coordinated vegetal movement until 85-90% epiboly, when detached cells reach ~80% and the cluster detaches from the EVL.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by immunostaining quantification (Figure 6C) showing temporal progression of attached/detached ratios. Claims C49-C51 provide time-lapse data (Figure 6D-F) identifying sources of detached cells and the critical threshold for cluster detachment. The data clearly demonstrate a transition point around 80% detached cells. However, the mechanism explaining how the cluster maintains coordinated movement with increasing detached cell proportion requires the E-cadherin results (next result) to be fully understood.

results.result: DFCs progressively cluster by decreasing inter-cell distance and increasing cell-cell contacts. E-cadherin is expressed and localized at DFC membranes, and its knockdown disrupts cluster cohesion, leading to multiple DFC racemes and significantly increased escape of detached cells toward the DCL. E-cadherin-mediated adhesion is necessary for recruiting detached DFCs into the vegetal motion of attached DFCs and for avoiding endodermal fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 provide quantitative clustering metrics (Figure 7A-D). Claims C54-C55 show E-cadherin expression/localization (Figure 7E, citing Kane et al., 2005). Claims C57-C58 provide functional evidence through morpholino knockdown (Figure 7F-H) showing disrupted cohesion and increased escape (statistically significant, p≤0.001). The dual function inference (C59, C79) is well-supported by the data. However, the morpholino approach has known limitations (off-target effects, incomplete knockdown), and genetic mutant validation would strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: In 43% of embryos, DFCs initially form 2-3 small clusters separated by ~50 μm that later coalesce. DFCs at cluster edges initiate adhesive contacts by sending long polarized protrusions that differ from other protrusions in length, lifetime, and alignment. Small DFC clusters with apical attachments begin detaching from extra-embryonic tissues only after initiating protrusion-mediated contacts with the central attached cluster, completing delamination when fully integrated.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 provide population-level data on cluster organization (Figure 8A-D). Claims C62-C63 provide quantitative protrusion analysis (Figure 8E-I) showing distinct properties of inter-cluster protrusions (statistically significant differences, p≤0.001 for length and lifetime). Claims C65-C66 provide temporal correlation data (Figure 8J, Figure 8—video 2) showing that delamination follows contact formation. The temporal sequence strongly supports the mechanistic coupling inference (C67, C83). This is a particularly elegant result showing coordination between adhesion and delamination.

results.result: Incomplete delamination serves as a cellular platform for coordinated tissue movements during development. The apical constriction process follows a temporal progression allowing long-term apical attachment retention. These attachments function as tissue connectors coupling DFCs with extra-embryonic tissue spreading, providing mechanical drag as the critical guidance mechanism rather than autonomous motility or contact-mediated repulsion.
results.evaluation: These claims synthesize the major findings into a unified model. The conclusion that mechanical drag provides critical guidance (C71) is well-supported by the convergence of correlation data (C27-C28), perturbation experiments (C30-C34), force transmission evidence (C35-C36), and attachment requirement (C37-C41). The contrast with prior hypotheses (C20, citing Ablooglu 2010 and Zhang 2016) is appropriate. The generalization to 'incomplete delamination as a platform' (C68, C72) is a reasonable inference but extends beyond the specific DFC system studied.

results.result: Asynchronous apical constriction generates two distinct DFC populations: attached cells pulled by extra-embryonic tissues and detached cells following through DFC-DFC contacts. This asynchrony potentially maintains a minimal number of attached DFCs to carry detached cells and may promote even dissipation of mechanical stress to protect epithelial integrity.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is well-supported by the data showing asynchronous delamination (C26) and the two-population model (C46-C51, C52-C67). However, claims C74-C75 are explicitly speculative ('potentially,' 'we can speculate'), lacking direct experimental evidence. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the observations, they represent future work rather than demonstrated results. The speculation about stress dissipation (C75) cites relevant literature (Heer and Martin 2017, Martin and Goldstein 2014) but lacks experimental validation in this system.

results.result: Migrasomes containing chemokine ligands Cxcl12a/b are enriched in the extracellular space surrounding DFCs, potentially explaining long polarized protrusions as a manifestation of chemoattraction.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 cites recent work (Jiang et al., 2019) showing migrasome enrichment, but C82 is explicitly speculative ('opening the possibility'). No experimental evidence is provided in this manuscript to test whether Cxcl12a/b guides the long protrusions. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work but is not a demonstrated result of the current study.

results.result: Small DFC sub-groups delaminate only after establishing adhesive contacts with the main cluster, suggesting mechanistic coupling between cell adhesion, motility, and delamination. E-cadherin mediates transfer of movement information between attached and detached DFC populations, representing a novel developmental function.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by the temporal correlation data (C65-C66, Figure 8J). Claim C84 synthesizes the E-cadherin results (C57-C59) with the population dynamics (C73). The inference of 'novel developmental function' is justified given the demonstrated role in motion transmission between populations defined by delamination state. However, the mechanistic details of how E-cadherin mediates force transmission remain unclear and would benefit from further investigation.

results.result: Motion transfer from attached to detached DFCs resembles leader-to-follower transmission in collective cell locomotion. E-cadherin's role in motion transmission complements its previously described function in clusterization, together ensuring progenitors reach the differentiation site in sufficient numbers as a tight collective.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 appropriately contextualizes the findings within the broader collective migration literature (citing Friedl and Gilmour 2009, Reig et al. 2014, Theveneau and Mayor 2013). Claim C86 integrates current findings with prior work (Hong and Dawid 2009, Matsui et al. 2011, Oteiza et al. 2010). The synthesis is well-supported and places the work in appropriate context. The comparison to leader-follower dynamics is apt given the attached/detached population structure.

results.result: The leader-to-follower locomotion mechanism operates until attached cells fall below ~20% (around 85-90% epiboly). After this stage, the DFC cluster loses YSL/EVL connections and begins internal reorganization toward rosette formation and organ differentiation, continuing vegetal displacement at slower speed while becoming covered by the DCL.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by the quantitative data (Figure 6E-F) showing the critical threshold. Claims C88-C89 cite prior work (Oteiza et al., 2008) for the subsequent developmental events and are supported by time-lapse data showing continued but slower movement. This appropriately defines the temporal limits of the described mechanism and connects to subsequent developmental stages.

results.result: Mechanical drag through adhesive contacts with moving tissues occurs in multiple developmental contexts: C. elegans primordial germ cells internalize through contacts with ingressing endoderm, killifish DCL spreads through contacts with expanding EVL, and zebrafish EVL spreading follows YSL movement through tight junction bonds.
results.evaluation: These claims cite appropriate literature (Chihara and Nance 2012, Reig et al. 2017, Behrndt et al. 2012, Betchaku and Trinkaus 1978, Koppen et al. 2006, Schwayer et al. 2019) to contextualize the findings within comparative developmental biology. The citations appear accurate and relevant. This appropriately positions the work as part of an emerging understanding of mechanical drag in morphogenesis.

results.result: Mechanical drag is an emergent mechanism of cell movement requiring further investigation. Drag-mediated locomotion is a crucial driver of organogenesis emerging at the embryonic/extra-embryonic interface, highlighting the essential role of mechanical information from extra-embryonic tissues in early development.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 appropriately identifies mechanical drag as an area for future investigation. Claim C94 synthesizes the findings and cites relevant literature (Christodoulou et al. 2019, Hiramatsu et al. 2013, Reig et al. 2017) supporting the broader importance of extra-embryonic tissues. While 'crucial driver' is a strong claim, it is reasonably supported by the demonstration that disrupting the mechanism prevents proper DFC allocation. The generalization is appropriate for a Discussion section.

results.result: DFCs move collectively from the embryo equator toward the vegetal pole, positioned ahead of the DCL margin. Despite sharing determinants with mesendoderm, DFCs remain separate from this domain. DFCs follow the same vegetal direction as the overlying EVL and show ZO-1-enriched puncta at the DFC-EVL and DFC-YSL interfaces, with marginal DFCs more abundant than submarginal DFCs.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the basic biological context and are well-supported by imaging data (Figure 1A-D) and appropriate citations (Cooper and D'Amico 1996, Oteiza et al. 2008, Pinheiro and Heisenberg 2020, Alexander and Stainier 1999, Warga and Kane 2018, Bruce and Heisenberg 2020, Ablooglu et al. 2010). The observations are clearly documented and provide essential background for the mechanistic studies. The quantification of marginal vs. submarginal DFCs (C9, Figure 1G) is statistically significant (p≤0.05).
